title: The printing press
deck: One workshop in Mainz in the 1450s. Presses in 236 European towns by 1500. Watch a machine for copying words spread across the map.
kidDeck: Before printing, every book was copied by hand. Then one workshop in Germany found a faster way. Watch the idea spread from town to town.

scenes.title: The *printing press*
text: Around 1440 the German goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg invented the movable-type printing press. Its spread brought an era of mass communication. Printed texts became cheaper and easier to find, and more adults learned to read.
This story first goes back to where printing began, far to the east. Then it follows the press out of one workshop in Mainz.
kid: Around 1440 a German goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg invented a machine for printing books. Books became cheaper, and many more people learned to read.
But printing itself began much earlier, far away in Asia. Let us start there.

scenes.title: A page carved in wood
text: Printing began in China, with woodblocks: a whole page carved into one block, inked, and pressed onto paper.
A copy of the Diamond Sutra found among the manuscripts of Dunhuang carries a date, 11 May 868. It is broadly considered the oldest printed book that survives, though earlier printed material exists.
kid: Printing began in China. A printer carved a whole page into a block of wood, covered it in ink and pressed paper onto it.
A printed Buddhist text found at Dunhuang in China has a date on it: the year 868. It is the oldest dated printed book in the world.

scenes.title: One piece for each character
text: Between 1039 and 1048 a Chinese artisan, Bi Sheng, invented the world's first movable type: small tiles of fired clay, one for each character, that could be set, printed and used again.
Bi Sheng was a commoner, and almost nothing is known of his life. His invention was recorded only in the Dream Pool Essays of the scholar-official Shen Kuo.
kid: About a thousand years ago, a Chinese craftsman named Bi Sheng had a clever idea. Instead of carving a whole page, he made a small clay piece for each character. The pieces could be put together to make a page, then taken apart and used again.

scenes.title: Metal type in Korea
text: In July 1377, at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju in Korea, a Buddhist anthology known as the Jikji was printed with metal type. It is the world's oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, 78 years older than Gutenberg's Bible.
Only the second volume of the metal printing survives. It is kept in the National Library of France.
kid: In 1377, at a temple in Korea, a book was printed using pieces of type made of metal. It is the oldest book of its kind that still exists, and it is older than Gutenberg's famous Bible.

scenes.title: A goldsmith in Mainz
text: Gutenberg's achievement was to make a system. He found a way to mass-produce metal type, casting it from an alloy of lead, tin and antimony. He used oil-based ink. And he built a wooden press similar to the agricultural screw presses of the time.
Movable type was already in use in East Asia. What Gutenberg's press brought was a much faster rate of printing.
kid: Gutenberg put several ideas together. He found a quick way to make lots of little metal letters. He used a thick, oily ink. And he built a wooden press that squeezed the paper down onto the letters.

scenes.title: The Bible, about 180 times
text: The first printing from the workshop that can be dated precisely is a church indulgence that existed by 22 October 1454. The first finished copies of the Bible were available in 1454 or 1455.
Either 158 or 180 copies were printed. Forty-nine survive at least in substantial part. It was the earliest major book printed in Europe with mass-produced metal movable type.
kid: Gutenberg's most famous book is a Bible in Latin, finished around 1455. He printed about 180 copies. Forty-nine of them still exist today.

scenes.title: Out of one workshop
text: At first Gutenberg's shop was the only one. Then the craft spread, with major towns as the centres: Cologne in 1466, Rome in 1467, Venice in 1469, Paris in 1470, Buda and Kraków in 1473.

By 1481 Italy and Germany each had print shops in about 40 towns. By 1500, 236 towns in Europe had presses, and an estimated twenty million books had been printed, for a population of perhaps seventy million.
kid: At first there was only one print shop. Then printers carried the idea from town to town. Watch the dots appear as you scroll.
By the year 1500, there were presses in 236 towns in Europe. They had printed about twenty million books.

sources.title: Global spread of the printing press

scenes.note: Only towns named in the source are marked. Hundreds more had presses by 1500.

scenes.title: Books that fit in a pocket
text: In Venice the printer and humanist Aldus Manutius founded the Aldine Press, devoted to publishing rare texts, among them Greek manuscripts. He introduced a small, portable book format, a forerunner of the modern paperback, and commissioned the typefaces that were the first known precursor of italic.
kid: In Venice, a printer named Aldus Manutius began to make small books that were easy to carry around. He also had a new slanted style of letters made, the first step towards the italics we use today.

scenes.title: Print and the Reformation
text: In 1517 Martin Luther, a professor at Wittenberg, wrote ninety-five theses against the sale of indulgences. They are seen in retrospect as the start of the Protestant Reformation. In September 1522 his German translation of the New Testament was published.
Printing let information move quickly across Europe, and it contributed to the Reformation and to the Scientific Revolution.
kid: In 1517 a teacher named Martin Luther wrote down his disagreements with the Church. Later he translated the Bible into German. Printing let new ideas travel fast.

scenes.title: The Earth moves, in print
text: In 1543 a press in Nuremberg printed On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres by Nicolaus Copernicus. It set out a model of the universe with the Sun at the centre, against the Earth-centred system that had been accepted since ancient times.
kid: In 1543 a book was printed in Nuremberg that changed how people saw the sky. Its writer, Copernicus, said that the Earth goes around the Sun, and not the Sun around the Earth.

scenes.title: Across the oceans
text: The press sailed with Europe's ships. Juan Pablos, a native of Lombardy, was the first documented printer in the Americas when he began printing in Mexico in 1539.

In 1556 Jesuits set up the first movable-type press in Asia at Goa. It had been meant for Abyssinia. In 1640 the Bay Psalm Book, the first book printed in British North America, came off a press in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
kid: Ships carried the printing press across the oceans. Printing began in Mexico in 1539 and in Goa, in India, in 1556. The press in Goa was supposed to go to Africa, but it never left India.
In 1640 the first book was printed in the English colonies of North America.

sources.title: Global spread of the printing press

scenes.title: Where the press was not welcome
text: The press did not spread everywhere at the same speed. According to some sources, printing in the Arabic script met strong opposition from legal scholars and manuscript scribes and stayed formally or informally prohibited in the Ottoman Empire between 1483 and 1729. Hebrew presses, meanwhile, worked in Constantinople as early as 1493.

Ibrahim Muteferrika, born in Hungary, was the first Muslim to run a press with movable Arabic type. He was given permission to publish non-religious books, and his first, an Arabic–Turkish dictionary, appeared in 1729.
kid: Not everyone wanted the press. In the Ottoman Empire, printing in Arabic letters was not allowed for a very long time. The people who copied books by hand were against it.
In 1729 a man named Ibrahim Muteferrika printed the first book there in Arabic letters. It was a dictionary.

sources.title: Global spread of the printing press

scenes.title: The first newspaper
text: In 1605 Johann Carolus of Strasbourg began to publish the Relation, an "account of all distinguished and commemorable stories". The World Association of Newspapers recognises it as the world's first newspaper.
kid: In 1605 a man in Strasbourg named Johann Carolus began to publish the world's first newspaper.

scenes.title: Faster and faster
text: Around 1600 a European press could make between 1,500 and 3,600 impressions in a working day. By then Europe's presses had produced an estimated 150 to 200 million copies.

In 1843 Hoe's rotary press allowed much higher output, and later rotary presses could print millions of pages a day. By the end of the 19th century, Western printing technology had been adopted all over the world.
kid: Presses kept getting faster. Around 1600 one press could print a few thousand pages in a day. Later machines could print millions.
By about 1900, printing presses were at work all over the world.

quiz.why: Woodblock printing began in China. The oldest dated printed book, from the year 868, was found at Dunhuang.

q: What were the first movable type pieces made of?
quiz.why: Bi Sheng made the first movable type from fired clay in China between 1039 and 1048.

q: By 1500, how many towns in Europe had printing presses?
quiz.why: From one workshop in the 1450s, printing spread to 236 European towns by the year 1500.
